title: Subject-Verb Agreement
notes: Subject-verb agreement is the grammatical rule that the verb must match its subject in number (singular or plural) and person (first, second, third). A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural verb. This is one of the most frequently tested grammar rules in NEB English exams, appearing in gap-filling, error correction, and multiple-choice questions.

The fundamental rule: Singular subjects take singular verbs (usually ending in -s in present tense). Plural subjects take plural verbs (no -s in present tense). Examples: 'The boy runs' (singular subject + singular verb). 'The boys run' (plural subject + plural verb). 'She is here' vs. 'They are here'. Note that the verb 'to be' is irregular: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, they are. This irregularity is a common source of errors.

When two or more subjects are joined by 'and', they usually take a plural verb: 'Rama and Shyam are friends.' 'The teacher and the principal are coming.' Exception: When the two nouns joined by 'and' refer to the same person or thing, use a singular verb: 'The singer and songwriter is performing tonight' (one person who is both singer and songwriter). 'Bread and butter is my favourite snack' (a single combination).

When subjects are joined by 'or', 'nor', 'either...or', or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject (proximity rule). Examples: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present.' (nearer subject 'students' is plural → plural verb). 'Either the students or the teacher is responsible.' (nearer subject 'teacher' is singular → singular verb). 'Neither Ram nor his friends are coming.' This proximity rule is consistently tested in NEB exams.

Most indefinite pronouns take singular verbs: each, every, either, neither, one, someone, somebody, something, anyone, anybody, anything, no one, nobody, nothing, everyone, everybody, everything. Examples: 'Each of the boys has a pen.' 'Nobody knows the answer.' 'Everyone is present.' However, 'both, few, several, many' take plural verbs: 'Both of them are coming.' 'Few of the students have passed.' 'Several of the books are missing.'

The words 'each' and 'every' always take singular verbs, even when followed by a plural noun in a prepositional phrase. 'Each of the students has a book.' (NOT 'have'). 'Every boy and girl has a seat.' (NOT 'have'). 'Each' emphasises individuality within a group; 'every' emphasises the group as a whole. Both require singular verbs because they refer to individuals one by one.

This is a classic NEB exam distinction. 'The number' is singular: 'The number of students is increasing.' (We are talking about the number itself — singular.) 'A number' is plural: 'A number of students are absent.' (We are talking about the students — plural.) Think of it this way: 'The number' = one specific figure (singular). 'A number' = several (meaning 'many') — plural.

Collective nouns (team, class, government, committee, herd, flock, jury, staff, family) can take either singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group acts as one unit or as individuals. Singular (unit): 'The team is winning.' (the team as one unit). Plural (individuals): 'The team are arguing amongst themselves.' (members acting individually). In American English, collective nouns tend to take singular verbs; in British English, both are acceptable depending on meaning. NEB exams generally follow British English conventions.

Expressions of money, distance, time, and weight treated as a single quantity take singular verbs: 'Ten rupees is not enough.' 'Five kilometres is a long walk.' 'Two hours is a long time.' 'Ten kilograms is too heavy.' However, when the individual items are emphasised, plural verbs may be used: 'Ten rupees are in my pocket' (the individual notes/coins). The singular form is far more common and is the expected answer in NEB exams.

With 'there' as a dummy subject, the verb agrees with the real subject that follows it. Singular: 'There is a book on the table.' Plural: 'There are books on the table.' When the subject is a compound joined by 'or/nor', the proximity rule applies: 'There is a pen and two books on the table' (nearer subject 'pen' is singular). 'There are two books and a pen on the table' (nearer subject 'books' is plural). This rule is consistently tested.

In relative clauses (who, which, that), the verb agrees with the antecedent (the noun the relative pronoun refers to). 'She is one of the students who study hard.' (who = students, plural). 'She is the only one of the students who studies hard.' (who = one, singular — 'the only one' changes the reference). 'This is the book that interests me.' (that = book, singular). The presence or absence of 'the only' before 'one' changes the antecedent and therefore the verb form.

Certain words are always grammatically singular and take singular verbs: each, every, either, neither, one, another, the other (when used as a pronoun). Also singular nouns ending in -ics when referring to an academic subject: physics, economics, mathematics, politics, linguistics. 'Physics is my favourite subject.' However, when -ics words refer to a physical activity or manifestation, they are plural: 'The politics of the country are unstable.' 'His manners are rude.' (manners is always plural).

Certain nouns are always plural in form and take plural verbs: scissors, trousers, glasses, shoes, pants, clothes, binoculars, pliers, tongs. 'My scissors are blunt.' 'The trousers fit well.' When referring to a single item, use 'a pair of': 'A pair of scissors is on the table.' (Here, 'pair' is singular, so 'is' is correct. But 'The scissors are' uses the plural noun directly.)
confusion: Each of the boys vs. Each boys: 'Each' is always followed by a singular verb, even when followed by 'of the + plural noun'. 'Each of the boys is here' (correct). 'Each of the boys are here' (wrong). The phrase 'of the boys' is a prepositional phrase modifying 'each'; the subject is 'each', which is singular.

The number vs. A number: 'The number' refers to a specific numerical value and is singular ('The number of applicants is 500'). 'A number' means 'several' or 'many' and is plural ('A number of applicants are waiting'). This distinction is frequently tested in NEB exams and is a common source of errors.

Neither...nor proximity rule: The verb agrees with the subject nearer to it, not the first subject. 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present' (students is nearer → plural). 'Neither the students nor the teacher was present' (teacher is nearer → singular). Students often incorrectly make the verb agree with the first subject instead of the nearer one.

One of the students who study vs. One of the students who studies: In 'She is one of the students who study hard', 'who' refers to 'students' (plural) → 'study'. In 'She is the only one of the students who studies hard', 'who' refers to 'one' (singular, because 'the only one' restricts the reference) → 'studies'. The word 'only' changes everything.

Bread and butter is vs. Bread and butter are: When two nouns joined by 'and' represent a single idea or are commonly paired together, use a singular verb. 'Bread and butter is my favourite snack' (a single dish). 'Fish and chips is a British classic' (a single meal). But 'Bread and butter are sold separately' (two distinct items being discussed) uses plural.

News is vs. News are: 'News' is an uncountable noun that is always singular in English, despite ending in -s. 'The news is bad' (correct). 'The news are bad' (wrong). Similarly: 'The series is popular', 'The ethics is important', 'The statistics is misleading' (when referring to the field of study, singular; 'The statistics are inaccurate' when referring to numerical data, plural).
practice: Fill in the correct verb: Each of the students ___ (have/has) a textbook. [Answer: has]
Fill in the correct verb: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ (was/were) present. [Answer: were — agrees with nearer subject 'students']
Fill in the correct verb: The number of applicants ___ (is/are) increasing. [Answer: is — 'the number' is singular]
Fill in the correct verb: A number of students ___ (is/are) absent today. [Answer: are — 'a number' means 'many', plural]
Fill in the correct verb: Bread and butter ___ (is/are) my favourite snack. [Answer: is — treated as a single item]
Fill in the correct verb: The news ___ (is/are) very disappointing. [Answer: is — 'news' is always singular]
Fill in the correct verb: The scissors ___ (is/are) on the table. [Answer: are — 'scissors' is always plural]
Fill in the correct verb: She is one of the students who ___ (study/studies) hard. [Answer: study — 'who' refers to 'students' (plural)]
Fill in the correct verb: There ___ (is/are) a pen and two books on the desk. [Answer: is — agrees with nearer subject 'a pen']
Fill in the correct verb: Physics ___ (is/are) an important subject. [Answer: is — academic subjects ending in -ics are singular]
universalFacts: Subject-verb agreement is a universal grammatical feature, but the complexity varies enormously across languages. English requires agreement in the present tense (he runs vs. they run), while Chinese has no subject-verb agreement at all.

Nepali has a complex system of verb agreement that matches the subject in person, number, and honorific level (मैंले, तपाईंले, हुनुहुन्छ), which is more nuanced than English agreement. This makes agreement errors in English less likely for Nepali speakers, but the rules are different enough to cause confusion.

The 'each of + plural noun' construction is particularly difficult for learners because the plural noun in the prepositional phrase tempts students to use a plural verb. The key is to recognise that 'each' is the grammatical subject, not the noun in the prepositional phrase.

In NEB English exams, subject-verb agreement questions typically carry 3-5 marks in gap-filling and error correction sections. Students lose marks frequently by choosing the verb based on the nearest noun rather than the actual subject.

The word 'news' is always singular in English despite its -s ending, which confuses many learners because it looks plural. This is because 'news' derives from 'news' (plural of 'new'), which evolved into a mass noun meaning 'information about recent events'.

Collective nouns reveal a fascinating difference between British and American English: American English consistently uses singular verbs with collective nouns ('The team is winning'), while British English allows both singular and plural depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individuals.
